items.title: One of the biggest barriers to Web3 adoption is still the wallet experience.
items.summary:
One of the biggest barriers to Web3 adoption is still the wallet experience.

For experienced users, managing private keys, signing transactions, and switching networks may feel normal. But for someone entering crypto for the first time, these steps can be confusing and sometimes intimidating.

This is why smart wallet technology is so important.

@startaleapp is working to make wallet interactions more accessible through features such as social login and passkey-based access.

The interesting part is that improving wallet technology doesn't just make things more convenient. It can change how people interact with the entire blockchain ecosystem.

When users spend less time worrying about technical barriers, they can focus more on discovering applications, managing assets, and exploring new opportunities.

Of course, convenience must always come with strong security and clear control over digital assets.

I believe the next generation of wallets will be judged not by how many features they offer, but by how naturally people can use them.

A wallet should be a gateway to Web3, not the biggest obstacle standing in front of it. 
@StartaleGroup

items.summary:
🔐 𝗧𝗥𝗢𝗡 𝗣𝗔𝗦𝗦𝗞𝗘𝗬𝗦: 𝗠𝗔𝗞𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗪𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗘𝗧 𝗔𝗖𝗖𝗘𝗦𝗦 𝗦𝗜𝗠𝗣𝗟𝗘𝗥 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗦𝗠𝗔𝗥𝗧𝗘𝗥

What if accessing a blockchain wallet felt as simple as unlocking your smartphone?
Web3 adoption depends not only on powerful technology but also on a smooth user experience.
TRON is exploring passkey-enabled smart wallets to make authentication more familiar, convenient, and accessible.

1️⃣ 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗣𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗸𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀

TRON DAO's technical guide, Signing TRON Transactions With a Passkey, introduces a way to authorize wallet activity using device-supported authentication.

🔹 Familiar Authentication: Users can authenticate through supported methods such as Face ID, Touch ID, or fingerprint recognition.

🔹 P256VERIFY Precompile: TRON provides the P256VERIFY precompile at address 0x100 to verify P-256 signatures on-chain.

🔹 Bridging Cryptographic Differences: Traditional TRON accounts use secp256k1, while modern device passkeys commonly rely on P-256 cryptography.

🔹 Smart Wallet Verification: P256VERIFY allows smart contracts to verify signatures generated through supported passkey authentication.

🔹 Simpler User Experience: This approach can reduce dependence on manually managing seed phrases during everyday wallet interactions.

2️⃣ 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗚𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗕𝗲𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗕𝗶𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝘀

One important technical detail is that verifying a signature does not automatically prove that the user approved the intended transaction. The operation digest must be securely connected to the WebAuthn challenge. The wallet also includes its address and chain ID in the digest, helping prevent signatures from being replayed across different wallets or networks. This distinction matters because authentication confirms control of a credential, while secure challenge binding connects that authentication to a specific operation. Strong implementation must protect both parts.

3️⃣ 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗗𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗧𝗼 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹-𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱 𝗪𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝘁𝘀

The reference implementation demonstrates how developers can explore this technology across different platforms. It includes a Next.js application for passkey registration and signing, a P256SmartWallet smart contract deployed on the Nile testnet, and native iOS and Android applications supporting passkey authentication.

The guide also highlights important production requirements, including account recovery, credential management, domain selection, and transaction fee abstraction. Passkeys are not a complete replacement for every wallet security or recovery mechanism, but they offer a promising way to reduce onboarding friction.

The bigger vision is to make Web3 feel more natural without overlooking security. By combining cryptographic verification with familiar device authentication, TRON is giving developers another tool to build accessible smart-wallet experiences.

Better accessibility, thoughtful security, and a smoother path into Web3.

items.title: WebAssembly Didn’t Miss the Moment. AI Was Just Late.
items.summary:
# WebAssembly Didn’t Miss the Moment. AI Was Just Late.

Share

A few years ago, WebAssembly was the format that let a game engine or a design tool like Figma run in your browser at near-native speed. It was designed around one very specific problem: Run code that you didn't review, from a source you don't fully trust — safely, instantly, and anywhere.

Now, think about what an AI agent does all day:

It writes a Python script to clean up a CSV. [...] It generates a function to call an API it found in the docs five seconds ago.

It tries something, fails, rewrites it, and tries again.

That’s code nobody reviewed, from a source nobody fully trusts, that needs to start instantly and run anywhere.

Sound familiar? The problem WebAssembly was built to solve is exactly the problem that agents just created.

Today, we're making two things official. [...] Akamai Agent Sandbox building blocks headed to Spin, the open source framework under Akamai Functions

## Why WebAssembly is a great fit for AI workloads

Where should agent-generated code run? It needs to be isolated, it needs to start fast, and it shouldn’t cost much to keep ready. Containers and VMs handle isolation well, but speed and cost are where they struggle.

WebAssembly flips that trade-off. Four properties matter most for AI and agent workloads:

items.title: What’s new in MLE 23.26.4: WebAssembly lands in Oracle AI Database | developers
items.summary:
With Release Update 23.26.4, it gains support for WebAssembly (Wasm) modules. The feature is available now on Autonomous Database, with other deployment options to follow shortly.

WebAssembly is a portable binary format for code that can run in different environments. Programs written in languages such as C, Rust, and Go can be compiled to Wasm. Now, suitable Wasm libraries can run inside Oracle AI Database and be called from MLE JavaScript. [...] To use a library, you can store its Wasm binary as an MLE module and load its JavaScript bindings as a JavaScript module. Your JavaScript code imports the Wasm module and calls the library’s functions. Those functions can then form part of an application’s database logic.

I’ll share more technical examples in the coming weeks. In the meantime, please head over to the MLE WebAssembly documentation. We also plan to update the MLE LiveLabs so you can try the feature without setting up anything! [...] What can you do with that? Image processing is one example: a Wasm library can resize an image stored in the database. Other tasks, such as optical character recognition, may also be possible with libraries whose Wasm modules and JavaScript bindings work in MLE.

# `csv` — CSV file reading and writing [¶](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html\#module-csv "Link to this heading")

**Source code:** [Lib/csv.py](https://github.com/python/cpython/tree/3.15/Lib/csv.py)

* * *

The so-called CSV (Comma Separated Values) format is the most common import and
export format for spreadsheets and databases. CSV format was used for many
years prior to attempts to describe the format in a standardized way in
[**RFC 4180**](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4180.html). The lack of a well-defined standard means that subtle differences
often exist in the data produced and consumed by different applications. These
differences can make it annoying to process CSV files from multiple sources.
Still, while the delimiters and quoting characters vary, the overall format is
similar enough that it is possible to write a single module which can
efficiently manipulate such data, hiding the details of reading and writing the
data from the programmer.

The `csv` module implements classes to read and write tabular data in CSV
format. It allows programmers to say, “write this data in the format preferred
by Excel,” or “read data from this file which was generated by Excel,” without
knowing the precise details of the CSV format used by Excel. Programmers can
also describe the CSV formats understood by other applications or define their
own special-purpose CSV formats.

The `csv` module’s [`reader`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.reader "csv.reader") and [`writer`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.writer "csv.writer") objects read and
write sequences. Programmers can also read and write data in dictionary form
using the [`DictReader`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.DictReader "csv.DictReader") and [`DictWriter`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.DictWriter "csv.DictWriter") classes.

See also

[**PEP 305**](https://peps.python.org/pep-0305/) \- CSV File API

The Python Enhancement Proposal which proposed this addition to Python.

csv.reader( _csvfile_, _/_, _dialect='excel'_, _\*\*fmtparams_) [¶](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.reader "Link to this definition")

Return a [reader object](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#reader-objects) that will process

A csvfile is most commonly a file-like object or list.
